newsitem.title: BELGIUM: MEPS, magistrates want cooperation on international crime.
newsitem.headline: MEPS, magistrates want cooperation on international crime.

text.p: European magistrates and MEPs urged European Union countries on Wednesday to remove the barriers preventing the judiciary from effectively tackling international crime.
"We think it is important to make cooperation at judicial level easier," French magistrate Renaud van Ruymbeke told a news conference in the European Parliament.
"As we can't work outside our national territory, we have found it difficult to work against international drug trafficking and money laundering," he said.
Ruymbeke was speaking after a hearing in the parliament at which six magistrates spelled out their "Geneva appeal".

The appeal, launched last October, calls for simple, swift procedures for magistrates to consult their counterparts abroad and investigate foreign bank accounts, and EU help for national criminal and financial investigations.
The original appeal was signed by seven magistrates, from Italy, France, Spain and Belgium, who are now garnering more signatures in their home countries.
Dietmut Theato, the German Christian Democrat chairwoman of the parliament's budget control committee, insisted there was a need for EU-level action to tackle EU-level crimes.
She said conventions between member states, such as the police cooperation agreement Europol, were inadequate because they were dependent on the erratic good will of the countries involved.
Italian Socialist Rinaldo Bontempi announced that as a follow up to the hearing MEPs would push for binding EU directives on combating fraud.

They would demand provisions for better judicial cooperation to be included in the EU treaty and they would launch a political campaign to persuade the member states to ratify and implement conventions which commit them to working together to combat crime.
Unfortunately the member states were so far unwilling to accept EU laws, even on matters of obviously common concern, like protecting the EU budget, Theato said.
"The member states have not yet understood they lose money when there is EU budget fraud," she said, citing losses in tax revenue and market distortions as two of the most obvious consequences.

Nor had they accepted the advantages of cooperating through Europol with the European Commission's anti-fraud unit UCLAF, even though this would permit member states and UCLAF to consult each other's data banks, Theato added.

She said if European cooperation could be made to work effectively on fraud, these same structures could later be extended to tackle political corruption, money laundering, drug trafficking and international paedophile rings.
Theato said sensitivities over sovereignty and the differences in national legal traditions meant it would be difficult to persuade member states to harmonise their legal systems.
But she agreed with the judges something must be done because criminals were running circles round the authorities.
"We should all be equal before the law but because of the lack of international cooperation...this is no longer true," Gherardo Colombo, Milan's assistant public prosecutor, told reporters.
"Some people are able to use international channels and interntational circuits so...you cannot apply the law," he said.
